n: Nephi comments on the prophecies of Joseph of Egypt that Lehi had just recited.

f.w: Joseph, who was carried into Egypt

n: Joseph prophesied about all his descendants, and few prophecies are greater. His writings, which included prophecies about Lehi’s people, were on the brass plates but are not in our Bible.

f.w: they are written upon the plates of brass

n: Lehi gathers Laman’s children to bless them, calling them the children of his firstborn.
Lehi repeats the Lord’s core promise: keep the commandments and prosper; disobey and be cut off from His presence.

f.w: ye shall prosper in the land

n: Lehi cannot die without blessing these grandchildren. He knows that children raised in the right way will not leave it.

f.w: brought up in the way ye should go

n: If these children are cursed because of their parents’ choices, Lehi blesses them so the curse may rest on the parents instead. Children are not held responsible for their parents’ sins.

f.w: be answered upon the heads of your parents

n: Because of this blessing, God will not allow them to perish and will be merciful to their descendants forever.

f.w: he will be merciful unto you and unto your seed forever

n: Next, Lehi calls Lemuel’s children before him.
He gives them the same blessing: they will not be entirely destroyed, and in the end their descendants will be blessed.

f.w: in the end thy seed shall be blessed

n: Lehi then speaks to Ishmael’s sons and their entire household. Their words are not recorded.
Lehi blesses Sam: he will inherit the land like Nephi, and his descendants will be counted with Nephi’s. Sam, the quiet faithful brother, shares Nephi’s blessings.
After blessing his whole household according to his heart and the Spirit, Lehi grows old, dies, and is buried. A great patriarch’s life ends.
Soon after Lehi’s death, Laman, Lemuel, and Ishmael’s sons grow angry with Nephi because of the Lord’s warnings he delivered.
Nephi felt compelled to speak to them by the Lord’s word. Much of what was said is recorded on his other (large) plates, which contain more history.

On these small plates Nephi writes the “things of my soul” and scriptures from the brass plates. He loves the scriptures, ponders them, and writes them for his children. This introduces what is often called the “Psalm of Nephi.”

f.w: my soul delighteth in the scriptures

n: Nephi delights in the things of the Lord and constantly ponders what he has seen and heard.
Despite God’s goodness, Nephi cries out, “O wretched man that I am!” He grieves over his weaknesses and sins. Even great prophets feel their imperfections deeply — Paul uses the same words.

f.w: O wretched man that I am

n: Nephi feels surrounded by temptations and sins that “easily beset” him — that cling and trip him up.
When he wants to rejoice, his heart groans over his sins — yet he knows whom he has trusted. That turning point changes everything.

f.w: I know in whom I have trusted

n: Nephi remembers God’s past help: support in trials, guidance through the wilderness, and protection on the ocean. Remembering builds hope.

f.w: the waters of the great deep

n: God has filled him with love so intensely that his body could barely bear it.
God confounded his enemies until they trembled before him.
God heard his cries by day and gave him visions by night.
In bold, mighty prayer Nephi has called on God, and angels have come down to minister to him.
Carried by the Spirit to high mountains, Nephi saw things too great for man to write.
Then why, having seen so much of God’s mercy, should he linger in sorrow and lose strength because of trials? Nephi questions his own discouragement.
Why give in to sin and temptation and let the evil one destroy his peace? Why be angry with his enemy? Nephi identifies anger as part of his struggle.

f.w: Why am I angry because of mine enemy?

n: Nephi rallies himself: “Awake, my soul!” He commands his heart to rejoice and give no place to the enemy.

f.w: give place no more for the enemy

n: He resolves not to be angry with enemies or lose strength because of afflictions.
He calls his heart to rejoice and praise the Lord forever, “the rock of my salvation.”
Nephi prays: redeem my soul, deliver me from my enemies, and make me “shake at the appearance of sin” — so sensitive that even the hint of sin makes him recoil.

f.w: shake at the appearance of sin

n: Nephi asks that hell’s gates stay shut to him because his heart is broken and his spirit contrite. He also asks God to keep him enclosed within “the gates of thy righteousness,” so he can walk the humble low road and stay strictly on the plain path.

f.w: my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite

f.g: A humble path, in contrast to proud heights.

n: Nephi asks to be wrapped in the “robe of righteousness,” to have an escape from enemies, a straight path, and no stumbling blocks — and for God to block his enemy’s way instead of his.

f.g: Don’t block my path with obstacles.

n: Nephi will trust God forever and never put his trust in the “arm of flesh” — human strength — for those who do are cursed.
God gives generously to those who ask, as long as they don’t ask for the wrong things. So Nephi will keep crying to God, his rock, forever.

f.w: God will give liberally to him that asketh
